Chapter 1: Witnessing a Changing World Through a Lifetime
Imagine stepping into the world as a child, everything around you feeling solid and everlasting. That’s how it was for one boy, growing up in the English countryside back in the 1930s. The fields seemed endless, woods alive with birdsong and the quiet rustle of little creatures. He’d spend hours searching for fossils, peering into ponds, and just soaking in the wildness that, to him, felt like it would last forever. Nature seemed infinite, something you’d never really question.
But as the years slipped by, that sense of permanence started to fade. The boy grew up, became a young man, and set off to explore the world—camera in hand—hoping to capture its wonders. He trekked through dense rainforests, sailed over glowing coral reefs, and watched whole herds of animals roam across vast plains. Every trip brought new marvels, but also subtle hints that things were changing.
Forests that once stretched beyond sight now stopped short—cut through by roads or replaced by fields. Rivers moved slower, sometimes clogged with silt or even pollution. And the animals? There just weren’t as many. Their homes were shrinking, and their numbers quietly dwindling.
Most folks didn’t notice these shifts right away. Life in towns and cities rolled on as usual. Supermarkets overflowed with food, new gadgets promised a better tomorrow. But for those out in the wild, the loss was obvious. The world was growing quieter, and emptier. That endless parade of life now seemed to be slipping away.
Even the countryside he once called home wasn’t immune. Hedges grew thinner, fewer birds filled the sky. The ponds where kids once caught newts had dried up or disappeared. These changes crept in slowly—almost too quietly to notice day by day—but they just didn’t stop.
Looking back, it’s clear that wildness was being swapped for something else: more farmland, bigger cities, new roads. People’s needs kept growing, and nature was squeezed to make room. It wasn’t any one person’s grand plan—just millions of small, everyday choices, each one making sense on its own, but together adding up to something huge.
Over the decades, the pace of change became impossible to ignore. Forests disappeared at an incredible speed. Oceans warmed and became more acidic. Entire species vanished—sometimes before anyone even got to know them. The world wasn’t being changed by nature, but by us.
For anyone who’d experienced the wild world up close, this loss hit home. It wasn’t just about numbers or news stories—it was about memories of places that no longer existed, animals that nobody would ever see again. The excitement of discovering new wonders was now mixed with sadness, and a growing urgency.
But here’s the thing—even with so much lost, there’s still hope. The world is still beautiful, still brimming with life. The real question is: will people notice what’s slipping away, and will we act in time to protect what we still have?
